questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Fossae and Spaces of the Upper Limb
questions.question: A 68-year-old woman sustained a fracture of the proximal humerus and injured the axillary artery. She began bleeding into the fascia around it. Where is this fascia derived from?

options.text: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia

questions.explanation: The fascia around the axillary vessels and brachial plexus is called the axillary sheath. It is derived from the prevertebral fascia. Clinical correlations in the source: in a brachial plexus nerve block the axillary sheath localizes anaesthetic solution to the plexus; a chronic retropharyngeal abscess in tuberculosis may spread to the axilla or superior mediastinum, but it never spreads to the posterior mediastinum because the supravertebral fascia fuses there to restrict spread.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Fossae and Spaces of the Upper Limb
questions.question: Identify the structure labelled in the diagram below.
questions.explanation: The labelled structure is the artery piercing the clavipectoral fascia, the thoracoacromial artery. Clavipectoral fascia envelops subclavius and pectoralis minor; medially it forms the costocoracoid ligament, and laterally it is connected to axillary fascia by the suspensory ligament of the axilla (Gerdy's ligament). Structures piercing clavipectoral fascia are one vein (cephalic vein), one artery (thoracoacromial artery with associated veins and lymphatics) and one nerve (lateral pectoral nerve).

questions.question: A patient presents with severe radicular pain of the upper extremity due to compression of the radial nerve in a space around the shoulder joint. Which of the following is false regarding this space?

options.text: Superior border is by teres major
It contains the circumflex scapular vessels
Lateral border is by shaft of humerus
Medial border is by long head of triceps

questions.correctAnswerText: It contains the circumflex scapular vessels
questions.explanation: The space around the shoulder joint where the radial nerve may be compressed is the triangular interval. It contains the profunda brachii vessels. Therefore, the statement that it contains the circumflex scapular vessels is false.

questions.chapter: Fossae and Spaces of the Upper Limb
questions.question: A 52-year-old woman presented with weakness of shoulder movements. Investigations revealed quadrangular space syndrome. Which of the following nerve is likely to be affected?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve is likely to be affected because it is one of the contents of the quadrangular space. Quadrangular space syndrome is caused by hypertrophy or fibrosis of quadrangular-space muscles, impinging on the axillary nerve and producing weakness of shoulder movements.

questions.chapter: Fossae and Spaces of the Upper Limb
questions.question: A patient presented with tenderness in the region shown below following a fall on an outstretched hand. Which of the following forms the roof of this region?
questions.explanation: The marked region is the anatomical snuffbox. The superficial branch of the radial nerve forms the roof. Tenderness here suggests scaphoid fracture, a common injury after a fall on an outstretched hand. Boundaries: lateral wall - abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis; medial wall - extensor pollicis longus. Roof - cephalic vein and superficial branch of radial nerve. Floor - radial styloid, scaphoid, trapezium and first metacarpal. The only content is the radial artery.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman presents with tingling and numbness in her hands. The symptoms get worse at night and when she's at work using her computer. The affected structure contains all of the following except:
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of carpal tunnel syndrome. The carpal tunnel does not contain flexor carpi ulnaris. Its contents comprise four flexor digitorum profundus tendons, four flexor digitorum superficialis tendons, one flexor pollicis longus tendon and the median nerve between the FDP and FDS tendons. Superficial to the carpal tunnel and flexor retinaculum, the ulnar artery and ulnar nerve pass through Guyon's canal.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Fossae and Spaces of the Upper Limb
questions.question: Which among the following is false regarding flexor retinaculum or transverse carpal ligament?

options.text: It is medially attached to pisiform and hook of hamate
It is laterally attached to scaphoid and trapezium
It splits into a medial superficial slip and a lateral deep slip
Flexor carpi radialis is the only content in the medial slip

questions.correctAnswerText: Flexor carpi radialis is the only content in the medial slip
questions.explanation: Flexor carpi radialis is the only content in the lateral deep slip of the flexor retinaculum, not the medial slip. The flexor retinaculum has a medial superficial slip (volar carpal ligament) forming Guyon's canal, which contains the ulnar nerve and vessels; and a lateral deep slip containing only the FCR tendon. Attachments are medial to pisiform and hook of hamate, and lateral to the tubercles of scaphoid and trapezium.

questions.question: Which of the following is not present in the fourth compartment of the extensor retinaculum?
questions.explanation: Extensor pollicis longus is not present in the fourth compartment of the extensor retinaculum. The extensor retinaculum attaches medially to pisiform and triquetral, and laterally to the anterior border of radius.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Fossae and Spaces of the Upper Limb
questions.question: Which of the following is false about dorsal digital expansion?

options.text: Base of the expansion is at the MCP
Wing tendons refer to the attachment of extensor digitorum
The central slip of the extensor tendon is attached to the base of middle phalanx
The collateral slips are attached to the base of distal phalanx

questions.correctAnswerText: Wing tendons refer to the attachment of extensor digitorum
questions.explanation: Wing tendons refer to the insertion of lumbricals and interossei to the corners of the dorsal digital (extensor) expansion or simply extensor expansion, not to the attachment of extensor digitorum. The expansion is formed by extensor tendons expanding on the back of digits; the apex is at the distal phalanx, central region attaches to the middle phalanx (in the thumb to proximal phalanx), and the base is at the sides of the MCP joint. The central and collateral slips distribute the extensor mechanism to middle and distal phalanges.

questions.chapter: Fossae and Spaces of the Upper Limb
questions.question: A patient presents with pain in one of her fingers. Kanavel's sign is positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kanavel's sign is suggestive of tenosynovitis. It helps distinguish infectious tenosynovitis from superficial or localized abscess. Kanavel's signs are tenderness over the affected tendon, fusiform swelling over the affected tendon, the affected finger held in slight flexion, and pain on passive extension.

questions.question: Which of the following is not the content of the mid-palmar space?
questions.explanation: The first lumbrical is not a content of the mid-palmar space. It is related to the FDP tendon of the index finger (second digit) and lies in the thenar space. The second, third and fourth lumbricals are related to the FDP tendons of the middle, ring and little fingers, respectively, and lie in the mid-palmar space.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.chapter: Fossae and Spaces of the Upper Limb
questions.question: A patient with the following infection in the finger requires incision and drainage as it can lead to all of the following except:

options.text: Necrosis of the whole of phalanx
Septic arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joint

questions.correctAnswerText: Necrosis of the whole of phalanx
questions.explanation: The image shows an infection of the pulp space of a finger, or whitlow. It requires incision and drainage because, if neglected, it can lead to necrosis of the distal 4/5th of the terminal phalanx. It does not cause necrosis of the entire phalanx because the proximal 1/5th is spared where the artery does not cross the fibrous septa. The pulp space contains subcutaneous fat arranged in tight compartments formed by fibrous septa from skin to periosteum. Complications include ischemic necrosis of the distal 4/5th of the terminal phalanx, osteomyelitis, flexor tenosynovitis and septic arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joint.
